blocks.content: Welcome to the Python course!
You're about to begin your journey with Python—one of the most popular and widely used programming languages in the world.
Python is easy to understand, yet powerful enough to build many different types of projects.
It is used to create websites and applications, analyze data, automate tasks, and even develop solutions using AI.
Whether you're planning to build a career in technology or simply want to explore programming, Python is a great language to begin with.
For now, you don't need to write any code on this page.
Take a look at the editor on the right. You'll soon use it to write and run your own Python code.
And don't worry about making mistakes—you're here to learn. Follow along, try things out, and feel free to explore.
This course will take you through Python step by step with simple explanations and practical learning. No prior programming experience is required.
When you're ready, click Next Lesson, and let's run your very first Python program together.

lessons.title: Strings are Fixed Values
lessons.summary: Do you remember the first Python program you created?

blocks.content: Do you remember the first Python program you created?
We asked you to write it exactly that way — and there is an important reason for it.
In Python, strings are case-sensitive. This means capital and small letters are considered different.
For example:

- "welcome to go coder" is not the same as "WELCOME TO GO CODER"
- "welcome to go coder" is not the same as "Welcome To Go coder"
- "welcome to go coder" is not the same as "WelCome To Go Coder"
Every letter must match exactly — including the spelling and capitalization.
Spaces are important as well.
Even one extra or missing space can make a string different.

- "welcome to go coder" is not the same as "welcome to go coder" (the spaces are different)
- "welcome to go coder" is not the same as " welcome to go coder" (there is a space at the beginning)
- "welcome to go coder" is not the same as "welcome to go coder " (there is a space at the end)
They may appear almost identical to us, but Python treats each one as a different value.
So, always check your spelling, capitalization, and spaces carefully.
Next, let's explore how numbers work in Python.

blocks.content: Python has two commonly used kinds of numbers:
Integers are whole numbers that do not have a decimal point. They may be positive, negative, or zero. Examples are 8, -15, 0, and 20.
Floating-point numbers include a decimal point. They can also be positive, negative, or zero. Examples are 3.5, 7.25, 0.0, and -4.8.

lessons.title: Python Comments
lessons.summary: In Python, the # symbol is used to add comments to your code.

blocks.content: In Python, the # symbol is used to add comments to your code.
In the previous lesson, we saw that writing something like this:
Will cause an error. This happens because Python tries to understand everything written on that line, including the extra text.
Sometimes, however, you may want to add a short note explaining what your code does. You can do this by using a comment.
Simply place a # before your note, like this:

blocks.starterCode: print(36.0) # this is the temperature

blocks.content: Now, Python runs print(36.0) and ignores everything written after the #.
Python also ignores any complete line that begins with #. Comments are not executed and do not appear in the output.

lessons.title: Legal Variables Names
lessons.summary: Python has some rules that you need to follow when naming variables. Let's take a look at them.

blocks.content: Python has some rules that you need to follow when naming variables. Let's take a look at them.
A variable name can contain only:

- letters
- numbers
- underscores
Spaces and other special symbols cannot be used in a variable name. If your variable name contains two words, you can separate them using an underscore _ or write them using camelCase.
For example, first name and first-name are invalid variable names. However, first_name and firstName are valid.

blocks.caption: Figure: Legal and Illegal Variable Names

blocks.content: Keep in mind that just because a variable name is valid does not mean it is a good choice. For example, abc is a valid name, but it does not clearly describe what the variable stores.
Refer to this [article](https://programiz.pro/resources/python-meaningful-variable-names/) to learn how and why you should assign clear and meaningful names to variables.

blocks.description:
Ready to become a triangle expert? Here's how it works:

This code helps you calculate the area of a triangle using the lengths of its three sides.

First, it prompts you to enter the lengths of the sides, then calculates the semiperimeter, which is half the sum of those lengths.

Using Heron's formula, it computes the area based on the semiperimeter and the side lengths. Finally, it prints the area for you.

What a neat way to bring geometry into coding! Keep practicing, and soon you'll be solving even more complex problems. What coding adventure will you tackle next?
blocks.code:
# Get the three sides of the triangle
a = int(input("Enter the first side: "))
b = int(input("Enter the second side: "))
c = int(input("Enter the third side: "))
# Calculate the semi-perimeter
s = (a + b + c) / 2
# Calculate and print the area
area = (s * (s - a) * (s - b) * (s - c)) ** (1/2)
print(area)
